pending_items.title: Egypt detains driver over Cairo fuel tanker fire that killed 31
pending_items.content:
Prosecutors in Egypt have ordered the detention of a 21-year-old driver suspected of causing a collision on Wednesday that overturned a fuel tanker on Cairo’s ring road, starting a fire that killed 31 people .

The Public Prosecution announced on Thursday that it had ordered the man to be held pending an investigation, and sent him to the Forensic Medicine Authority for tests to determine whether he had taken drugs.

The tanker burst into flames at about 6:30pm (16:30 GMT) on Wednesday, at the height of the evening rush hour, on an elevated stretch of the ring road in al-Waraq, a densely populated district of Giza on the western edge of the capital. The fire spread to passing traffic and destroyed 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles.

In an earlier statement, prosecutors said the driver told investigators he had been travelling from al-Marg towards al-Haram at 110km/h (68mph), with his father in the car, and was switching lanes to overtake other vehicles when the front left of his car struck the rear right of the tanker.

The man told prosecutors he then lost control and his car veered to the far right of the road. One of the tanker’s tyres burst, the statement said, before the vehicle hit a concrete barrier and overturned. Petrol leaking from the truck caught fire.

Prosecutors said they identified the driver after inspecting the scene and interviewing witnesses, and had since spoken to all the injured whose condition allowed them to be questioned. Forensic teams are taking DNA samples from victims’ relatives to identify some of the bodies. Relatives posted appeals on Facebook for men who had been on the road and had not been heard from since, the Reuters news agency reported.

The investigation will determine whether the driver bears criminal responsibility.

The Ministry of Health and Population on Thursday put the final toll at 31 dead and 26 injured, up from the 21 injured it had reported on Wednesday. Five of the injured have left hospital. The other 21 are still being treated, including eight transferred to other hospitals for further care. The bodies of the dead are in the custody of prosecutors, the ministry said.

By Thursday morning, traffic was moving again after crews cleared most of the burned wreckage. Salah Ahmed, a microbus driver, told the AP news agency that he had been on the ring road when the tanker caught fire but was held back by traffic, which saved his life.

“It was God’s hellfire on the ring road,” he said. “Why is a truck like this on the ring road at a rush hour? Who gets penalised for this happening?”

A 2018 cabinet decision barred trucks carrying more than four tonnes from the ring road between 6am and midnight, the AFP news agency reported. Prosecutors have not said why the tanker was on the road at the time.

“The tanks were exploding, the tyres were exploding, and there was fire,” Zaghlol al-Me, a local resident who reached the scene shortly after the crash, told Reuters. “We just didn’t know what to do or how to save anyone.”

The Public Prosecution’s statements are the first official account of how the crash happened. Early reports in local media suggested that a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the tanker. On Wednesday night, the Ministry of Transport denied issuing any statement to that effect and said the cause was a matter for prosecutors.

The Ministry of Electricity and Renewable Energy said the overhead lines were taut when the fire began and that two circuits tripped only after it started. The ministry’s spokesman, Mansour Abdel Ghani, told the Egyptian Youm7 daily newspaper that the lines had no connection to the crash and melted in the heat. A high-voltage line lay twisted on the ground on Thursday, AP reported.

President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi ordered full medical care for the injured and support for the families of those killed. Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly visited the injured on Thursday with Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar and Social Solidarity Minister Maya Morsy. Madbouly said the government, civil society and businesspeople would provide bank investment certificates to give bereaved families a stable income, and replacement vehicles for people whose cars burned.

“We realise that no compensation or money can make up for those we have lost,” Madbouly said.

Egypt’s Ministry of Social Solidarity said on Thursday that people could donate through the InstaPay app to help the injured and the families of those killed. It also opened an account at Nasser Social Bank for donations from businesses and civil society groups. The cabinet said the ministry had received 24 million Egyptian pounds (about $445,000) from seven charities.

The crash has renewed questions about road safety in Egypt. The Ministry of Transport says it spent about $37bn on transport between 2014 and 2024, yet 5,829 people were killed on the country’s roads in 2025, up 10.8 percent from the year before, and about 84,000 were injured, according to the state statistics agency, CAPMAS.

Egyptian legislators demanded accountability on Thursday. Mahmoud Samy, an MP, said the government needed to move from “building roads and expanding them to managing their safety professionally”. Abdel Moneim Imam, a politician who chairs the liberal Justice Party, said the cabinet bore full responsibility and should resign.

Amr Moussa, Egypt’s former foreign minister and former secretary-general of the Arab League, also criticised what he described as a deterioration in government oversight.

“Trading accusations and evading responsibility leads to the next disaster,” Moussa said, according to Reuters.

Transport Minister Kamel al-Wazir was appointed in 2019 after a train crash at Cairo’s Ramses station triggered a fire that killed 25 people, according to Reuters. He has rejected calls to resign since then, including after a lorry crash in the Nile Delta that killed 19 people, almost all of them young women, last year. The ministry declined to comment further when contacted by Reuters.

Earlier this month, a train crash, also in Giza, killed at least seven people and injured more than 125, prompting calls from legislators for accountability over recurring transport accidents.

pending_items.title: Sex, drugs, Israeli tech and Trump rivalries: Five explosive claims from Kushner-UAE book
pending_items.content:
An explosive new book by veteran journalist Matthew Cole claims Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and Middle East envoy, had a deep entanglement with the governments of Saudi Arabia and particularly the UAE, during the first Trump administration.

The book's most explosive claim is that Kushner was given approximately $2bn from the Saudi and Emirati governments, including $750m held at First Abu Dhabi Bank through an Emirati charity, Watani Al Emarat Foundation, ostensibly to support civic programs in the Emirates, but in reality used for Emirati weapons purchases and covert military operations.

Kushner, who is currently acting as an envoy for Trump in Ukraine and the Middle East, has vociferously denied the claims.

But the New York Times said the allegations against Kushner should be investigated when Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.

The book, Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East, published last month, contains dozens of other juicy nuggets about the Middle East and the wheeling and dealing that takes place in the region. It also provides a window into the culture of the UAE’s ruling Al Nahyan family.

Cole’s sources are anonymous and MEE couldn’t independently verify all the claims but has selected several highlights below.

Cole claims that in the 1990s, UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan hired two Syrians to film his brother and rival for the throne, former President Khalifa bin Zayed, having gay sex in a hotel room in southern Europe. Mohammed Bin Zayed then had Russian handlers deliver the tape to the brothers’ father - and founder of the UAE - Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, to embarrass Khalifa.

Cole wrote that Zayed bin Sultan realised Mohammed was trying to blackmail his brother, but appreciated his “cunning” and was “amused”. Cole says, “Within the Al Nahyan family, Mohamed’s blackmail attempt came to be seen as an early sign of his ambition to rule the UAE”.

Khalifa had only one wife and eight children, which was relatively rare for Gulf royals in the 1990s, but has become more common today.

Although Cole’s reporting on Khalifa bin Zayed’s sexual orientation has not been verified elsewhere, there are other reports of homosexuality among Gulf royals being used against them that have appeared in recent books on the Gulf.

Cole says Mohammed bin Zayed was also seen as hostile to former Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Nayef, who was eventually sidelined by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

According to Cole, Mohammed bin Zayed lobbied the US against Mohammed bin Nayef, on the basis of his alleged homosexuality.

In the case of Mohammed bin Nayef, his sexual orientation has been reported in two well-regarded books on the Saudi kingdom: New York Times Journalist Ben Hubbard’s MBS: The Rise to Power of Mohammed bin Salman and Blood and Oil: Mohammed bin Salman's Ruthless Quest for Global Power, by journalists Bradley Hope and Justin Scheck.

Khalifa bin Zayed became president of the UAE in 2004 after his father’s death. Despite his official title, he widely deferred to his brother, Mohammed bin Zayed, who was crown prince of Abu Dhabi, the UAE’s wealthiest emirate.

Khalifa bin Zayed’s decision to take a back seat to his ostensibly junior brother was often framed in the media as a willing decision that was eventually necessitated by a 2014 stroke he suffered.

Instead, Cole claims that he suffered from alcoholism and an “undiagnosed mental illness” long before. He says that when Mohamed bin Zayed was named deputy crown prince of Abu Dhabi in 2003, he was already providing medical treatments to his brother which left him unable to function.

“Khalifa’s medical treatment left him in a stupor, eventually causing nerve damage,” Cole wrote.

Cole suggests that Mohammed bin Zayed saw the treatment as a way to “undermine” his brother, and often forced the treatment on him with the help of an American nurse with whom he had a family connection.

According to the book, Mohammed bin Zayed had a sexual relationship with the nurse’s niece, Lisa, with whom he fathered an illegitimate child raised in Southern California.

The UAE is Israel’s closest Arab partner. The two were understood to have enjoyed close security ties for decades before the UAE joined the US-backed Abraham Accords in September 2020, making their relationship public.

The UAE has moved closer to Israel amid the US-Israeli war on Iran. The two countries are aligned in regional hotspots like Somaliland and Ethiopia as well.

Cole says that Mohammed bin Zayed was an admirer of Israel since at least the 1990s, despite his father’s reluctance to embrace Israel due to his sympathy with the Palestinians.

In 1998, after reading in Aviation Week about a new F-16 that the US had produced with Israeli software, Mohammed bin Zayed lobbied his father to purchase the warplanes. At the time, Mohammed bin Zayed was the UAE Armed Forces chief of staff and negotiated the purchase with the US.

With Mohammed bin Zayed’s backing, the UAE agreed to purchase 80 aircraft and install Israeli software in them. The decision came amid secret Israeli-Emirati discussions hosted by the Clinton Administration aimed at addressing Israel’s concerns that the sale would endanger its Qualitative Military Edge (QME).

The UAE’s decision to move closer to Israel publicly also sparked a crackdown at home. Cole wrote that Emirati poet Habib Al Sayegh was tortured to death in 2019, after writing a column against normalisation with Israel.

Sayegh was an Emirati luminary who even defended the UAE and Saudi Arabia’s blockade against Qatar. He was very much a member of the UAE’s state-backed elite, working as an editor at the Al Khaleej newspaper and serving as secretary general of the Arab Writers Union, according to the book.

Sayegh, however, was vocal in elite circles about the UAE’s growing closeness to Israel. Despite warnings to remain silent, in August 2019 he wrote a column titled “Israel Is Our Real Enemy and A Dangerous Project”.

Following publication of the article, Sayegh was abducted from his home by security officers at the orders of Mohammed bin Zayed, Cole writes. He says he was tortured with a pair of pliers used to pull out several of his teeth by one security agent, while another whipped him with a “belt-like strap with a sharp metal piece attached”.

Sayegh was beaten for three days. When he died, one of Mohammed bin Zayed’s closest aides described his body as “almost unrecognizable,” Cole writes.

Sayegh’s dissent stood in the way of a major diplomatic deal that Mohammed bin Zayed was discussing with Kushner and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Saudi Arabia would eventually grow cool on normalisation with Israel, but the agreement was for the Gulf states to recognise the country and sideline the Palestinians.

Jordan was envisioned as hosting the vast majority of three million Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank, thereby reducing the territory’s population by 90 percent. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would then recognise a rump Palestinian state, Cole wrote. The state would also be awarded some land in the Negev desert and Jordanian territory.

Cole’s book not only offers a window into the lives and ambitions of Gulf rulers, but also into key figures in the Trump administration. While some of the officials are not in government today, many of them remain central officials in the Middle East.

Besides Jared Kushner, the book discusses Tom Barrack at length. Barrack, a Lebanese-American former private equity investor, is currently US ambassador to Turkey and envoy to Iraq and Syria.

Barrack came under fire in the first Trump administration for initiating contact between Trump and the rulers of the UAE and Saudi Arabia before he took office. The book discusses those ties at length, but also suggests that Barrack grew frustrated with Kushner’s rise in the administration.

According to Cole, Barrack wanted to create a Marshall Plan - a reference to the post-WWII fund that rebuilt Europe - for the Middle East, funded by Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, to help develop the region.

But Kushner would only permit Barrack to handle the “Egyptian part” of the Middle East. Barrack would later lobby the UAE to tell Kushner that the Gulf state wanted him as Middle East envoy.

“The message to Barrack was clear: Kushner wouldn’t share White House relationships with MBS and MBZ,” Cole wrote, referring to Mohammed bin Salman and Mohammed bin Zayed.

Barrack and Kushner clashed again when Saudi Arabia and the UAE launched a blockade against Qatar in June 2017. At the time, Riyadh and Abu Dhabi were aligned, although they have more recently fallen out over Yemen, the Iran war and the Red Sea.

Despite his business ties with Saudi Arabia and the UAE, Barrack also tried to maintain good ties with Qatar.

According to the book, when the UAE and Saudi Arabia lobbied Kushner to support the blockade, Barrack joined former Secretary of State Rex Tillerson in pressing Trump not to join.

pending_items.title: Iran faces global condemnation over Kuwait attack that killed two Italians
pending_items.content:
Kuwait’s defense ministry said its forces intercepted several drones and that falling debris struck four people at a military site. The two Italians died of their injuries. A Kuwaiti army captain and a Pakistani national were also wounded.

The technicians worked for Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian arm of the German defense company. They were servicing radar antennas for a Skyguard air defense system used by Kuwait’s armed forces, Italy’s foreign ministry said.

Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said Rome would lodge a complaint with the Iranian embassy. He urged restraint, saying the Arab countries across the Persian Gulf from Iran were not parties to the war.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged greater pressure on Tehran to end attacks on its neighbors, saying security in the Persian Gulf “is a matter of security for us all.”

pending_items.title: شیوع آنفلوآنزا در بیشتر استان‌های ایران از آستانه هشدار عبور کرد
pending_items.content:
آمیتیس رمضانی، رییس انجمن متخصصان عفونی و عضو هیات علمی انستیتو پاستور ایران، پنج‌شنبه پنجم آذر در گفت‌وگو با خبرگزاری ایلنا گفت شمار مبتلایان به آنفلوآنزا و سرعت افزایش موارد جدید ابتلا در مقایسه با مدت مشابه سال گذشته بیشتر شده است.

او با اشاره به تغییر الگوی شیوع آنفلوآنزا در ایران گفت برخلاف سال‌های گذشته که در این مقطع زمانی آنفلوآنزای نوع «آ» غالب بود، اکنون بیش از ۷۰ درصد موارد ابتلا مربوط به نوع «بی» و حدود ۲۰ تا ۳۰ درصد مربوط به نوع «آ» است.

رمضانی افزود در بیشتر کشورهای جهان همچنان موارد ابتلا به آنفلوآنزای نوع «آ» در حال افزایش است، اما سرعت ورود ایران به موج آنفلوآنزا در مقایسه با سایر کشورها بیشتر است.

او از ابتلای قبلی به کرونا، تغییرات اقلیمی، شرایط آب‌وهوایی و تغییر الگوی سفرها به‌عنوان عوامل احتمالی موثر بر تغییر الگوی گردش ویروس‌ها نام برد.

به گفته رمضانی، موارد ابتلا به کرونا و آنفلوآنزا در مهر و نیمه نخست آبان به‌طور هم‌زمان افزایش یافت، اما در هفته‌های اخیر موارد ابتلا به کرونا کاهش یافته و روند شیوع آنفلوآنزا همچنان صعودی است.

رمضانی ۱۳ آبان نیز از افزایش هم‌زمان موارد ابتلا به کرونا و آنفلوآنزا در ایران خبر داده و اعلام کرده بود سهم نمونه‌های مثبت کرونا به حدود ۱۷ تا ۱۸ درصد رسیده و ویروس آنفلوآنزای نوع «بی» نیز در کشور غالب شده است.

افزایش ابتلا به آنفلوآنزا در میان کودکان

رییس انجمن متخصصان عفونی ایران، حضور دانش‌آموزان در مدارس و تماس نزدیک و مستمر آن‌ها با یکدیگر را از دلایل افزایش شیوع آنفلوآنزا در میان کودکان دانست.

او همچنین گفت کاهش تعاملات اجتماعی کودکان در دوران همه‌گیری کرونا ممکن است موجب شکل‌گیری ایمنی ضعیف‌تر در برابر برخی ویروس‌های تنفسی شده باشد.

رمضانی افزود احتمال بروز بیماری شدیدتر در کودکان نیز وجود دارد، هرچند شدت بیماری به عواملی از جمله سن، بیماری‌های زمینه‌ای، وضعیت واکسیناسیون و نوع ویروس بستگی دارد.
